en: Shi Dunlun’s *Collected Exegesis on the Treatise*, Fascicle Fifty-nine.
The preceding section concludes the first two of the three gates explaining the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*). From here below:
The third section explains the meaning of the nine gates.
Within this, first the nine gates are explained individually, and subsequently they are summarized in verse.
Regarding the former, the nine gates are initially explained.
The concluding section on the remaining categories of phrases does not appear here.
Regarding the first of the preceding sections, which clarifies the gateway of initiating karma, Jing says:
If one follows the Hīnayāna, it is said that the afflictions which give rise to karma are those directed toward external objects (*bahir-mukha-kleśa*).
If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* or the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, [the view is as follows].
Furthermore, karma is initiated by the non-shared ignorance associated with suffering.
As the Abhidharma states:
"Due to worldly delusion, one performs unwholesome karma."
Because of delusion regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha), one creates meritorious and immovable karma.
This passage explains that karma is initiated by ignorance (avidyā) which is deluded with respect to suffering (duḥkha). Why is this so?
Unwholesome [karma] brings about painful feeling;
this is precisely the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā).
This suffering of suffering is designated as the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya).
If one understands the conventional as conventional suffering,
yet remains deluded regarding this conventional suffering,
one creates unwholesome karma.
Wholesome karma brings about the experience of pleasure and equanimity within the realms of humans and devas;
this constitutes the essence of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Based on this suffering of conditioned existence, the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is established.
Only the Noble Ones (*ārya*) fully comprehend it as ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*).
Because one does not understand that pleasure, equanimity, and so forth are ultimately suffering, one creates meritorious and immovable karma.
The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that non-associated ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) is capable of giving rise to all karmas.
This applies to all four truths.
The unique ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*) is capable of initiating karma;
however, for one who has attained the fruit of training (*śaikṣa-darśana-mārga*), the fetter (*paryavasthāna*) of longing for future existence never arises again.
Regarding the occurrence of subsequent existence:

Question—Just as the karma produced by the afflictions of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) is abandoned through cultivation, is the karma produced by the afflictions of seeing (darśana-heya) abandoned through the path of seeing? Answer: Yes.

Answer: If it is already taught that even the retribution of the evil destinies is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), what fault would there be in [the view] that karma which is common to both [types of abandonment] is also abandoned by insight?
This present text states that all ten fundamental types of karma are initiators of action.
Alternatively, it may refer specifically to the ten afflictions underlying the truth of suffering; it may also refer generally to the ten afflictions underlying all four truths;
or it may refer generally to the ten fundamental afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Because both [the paths of] seeing and cultivation give rise to all [defilements],
it is said that "all can give rise to them. Although it is stated that both seeing and cultivation give rise to them, [this refers to the fact that]...
It is not yet known what kind of affliction gives rise to unwholesome karma that leads to rebirth in the evil destinies;
therefore, it is stated next that it is a "fierce" [affliction] capable of generating karma, rather than those [afflictions] that manifest through mere loss of mindfulness.
That is to say, karma of the superior grade, generated by intense and sharp afflictions,
leads to rebirth in the evil destinies; whereas karma generated by weak or middling-grade afflictions due to a lapse of mindfulness does not lead to the evil destinies,
but rather results in the experience of specific retributive suffering among humans and devas.
Furthermore, those karmas arising from discrimination are mostly of the superior grade and produce karma for rebirth in the evil destinies;
those produced spontaneously are mostly of the middling or inferior grades and result in rebirth among humans or devas. Tai says:
The *Old Śatyaśāstra* says:
"If there were no ignorance, the formative forces would not arise;
if there were no cultivation of the path, the formative forces would not ripen."
Now it is said:
"All [afflictions] are able to initiate [karma]. How is this to be reconciled? The explanation is:
if the afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya*) have not yet been abandoned, the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) will also initiate karma.
Once the delusions of views have been severed, cultivation cannot arise because there is no accompanying support.
For this reason, the author of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* says:
If one asks whether ignorance at the lower levels also initiates karma through the afflictions of view and so forth during the stage of cultivation,
this author of the treatise explains that all [levels] initiate karma. Furthermore, it is understood thus.
The afflictions of the path of seeing can project and complete karma;
this is the sense in which the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* treats them.
The afflictions of the path of cultivation can only project and complete karma.
Just as with the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and others who perform the "folding" (*paryanka-bandha*) and so forth, this author of the treatise [formulates his argument] based on this meaning.
If that is so, why does the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* state: "By means of mental reflection (*manasikāra*), various karmas are produced"?
"Due to the afflictions of views, the various formations reach maturity.
He then reflected on this further, saying:
"It is fully explained thus:"
In the Mahāyāna principle, for the most part, the delusions of view (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) initiate karma, while the delusions of cultivation (bhāvanā-kleśa) moisten it;
this is the same as the interpretation of Guṇavarma. Jì says:
This applies to both the paths of seeing and cultivation; since,
in the path of seeing, [the afflictions] of the desire realm are exclusively unwholesome,
they are all capable of initiating karma.
Regarding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), as stated in the *Abhidharma* (the *Abhidharmakośa*,
Chapter 4): "That which spontaneously gives rise to unwholesome conduct is unwholesome (*akuśala*)."
That is to say, since [afflictions] such as the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) are incapable [of producing new karma],
the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is termed the "discriminative" affliction.

As stated in the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmapada*, based on this principle, the karma for the three miserable destinies is produced [by the path of seeing] and not by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
However, this is discussed on the basis of projecting and completing results (*ākṣepaka-phala* and *paripūraka-phala*).
What prevents there also being karma that produces distinct retributions for the miserable destinies within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
Therefore, it is known that the present discussion concerns projecting results and does not concern completing results.
The second is the section on the explanation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Within this, first there is the correct determination of the characteristics;
subsequently, there is the conclusion of the preceding discourse’s intent to introduce the following section.
In the first part, the initial question and answer set forth the three characteristics;
subsequently, they are explained in sequence.
First, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is explained.
Because each abides in its own nature,
next the common characteristic is explained:
that which is not supremely tranquil is called the common characteristic of all afflictions.
In contrast to the preceding discussion on pure phenomena (*viśuddha-dharma*), it was stated that non-quiescence constitutes their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thirdly, the distinctions are explained:
first, the two gateways are questioned, and subsequently, those two gateways are explained.
The characteristics of the distinctions among the gates are as indicated in the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
Within the section on the distinctions of transformation (*parāvṛtti*), seven gates are first enumerated,
followed by an explanation of these seven gates.
This is divided into four sections.
The first explains the mode of activity of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). First, the characteristics of the latent dispositions are distinguished.
Subsequently, as the discussion unfolds, the analysis will be expanded upon the basis of its breadth and gravity.
Within the preceding eighteen [topics], they are collectively organized into eight pairs:
first, the pair of self and other objects.
Second, the pair of impairment and non-impairment;
third, the pair of increase and non-increase;
fourth, the pair of possession and non-possession.
5. The pair of harm and non-harm;
6. The pair of increase and so forth, and superiority and inferiority;
7. The pair of awakening and non-awakening.
Regarding the correspondence between the quantity of births and suffering:
that which follows its own object refers to the bondage of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of one's own stage to the objects of one's own stage.
Regarding "pursuing other objects": for example,
one born in a higher stage is pursued by the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the lower stages,
and one born in a lower stage is pursued by the latent dispositions of the higher stages.
Those that are impaired are, for example, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm suppressed by relying on the first dhyāna.
Those that are not impaired refer to the latent tendencies of the first dhyāna’s own level, whether one has already abandoned desire or has not yet abandoned it.
Regarding "increasing accordingly" (anuvṛddhi):

this means that because the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of their own respective stages repeatedly infuse [the mind], they increase. Regarding "not increasing accordingly": [this refers to those dispositions that do not so infuse].
This means that because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of one's own level or other realms are not repeatedly perfumed, they do not increase.

Regarding those who are incomplete [in their realization], according to the principles of the Mahāyāna, at the time of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), the seeds of affliction (*kleśa-bīja*) are already absent.
Therefore, there is no noble one who possesses full fetters, which differs from the *Kṣudraka-śāstra*.

Those who have awakened regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) refer to those for whom the results of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) operate simultaneously with the envelopments themselves.
The envelopments are the fruits of the perfuming agent.
That which coexists with the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of the perfuming agent is called "awakened.
That which is not awakened refers to that which is capable of producing [results] without coexisting with active outbursts.
Regarding the phrase "abounding in suffering," this means that the desire realm possesses all three types of suffering.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are two types of suffering; in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is only one.
From the eighth stage upward, they are called sovereign bodhisattvas (vaśitā-prāpta-bodhisattva).
Next, the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) are explained.

First, it is established through question and answer that the heavy residues belonging to the category of afflictions (*kleśapakṣa*) should be said to be distinct from the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in their active manifestation (*samudācāra*);
for even though an Arhat has already severed the heavy residues, the various formations (*saṃskāra*) still arise.
Master Ji says: "In this context, with reference to the nature of the *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness/heaviness),
this *dauṣṭhulya* is also called an *anuśaya* (latent tendency)."
Because this is of the nature of affliction (*kleśa*),
it is said that its essence is designated as "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*);
it is not called "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) by way of being a lack of stability.
Next, the eighteen types of *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness) are distinguished through a series of questions and answers.
Regarding the first six types of *dausthulya*,
there are three explanations from the Western [tradition].
The first protector of the Dharma says:
"The first three refer to naturally existing seeds (*dharmatā-bīja*),
while the latter three refer to newly perfumed seeds (*navasaṃskṛta-bīja*)."
The second, Candragupta, says:
"The first three refer to the seeds (bīja), while the latter three refer to the manifest (vartamāna).
The third, Jayasena, says:
The first three have been perfumed since beginningless time;
the latter three consist of present seeds. Jing says:
The first three [categories] refer to the heaviness (*dausthulya*) of all afflictions, karma, and retribution;
the next three refer exclusively to the heaviness of the three obstructions and the pervasive heaviness—
the heaviness that belongs to the five pervasive categories.
In the ninth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, twenty types of *dausthulya* (dysfunctions) are explained;
by adding the *dausthulya* of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the *dausthulya* of the meditative obstructions (*samāpattyāvaraṇa*),
these constitute eighteen types of *dausthulya*.
As in the preceding *Maulī Bhūmi*,
the second set of four turnings refers to the locations where they were previously and subsequently taught.
This refers to summarizing the second and third turns [of the wheel of Dharma],
which will be analyzed respectively in the seventh and eighth sections below; therefore,
it is mentioned here as a reference to what follows.
Therefore, it is said that one should extensively proclaim [this] in its own place.
The fourth chapter, on the transformation of distinctions,
should be understood as being like the skillful exposition of the aggregates (*skandha*).
The fifth [topic], regarding the power and lack of power of the afflictions, is also as explained in the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
The third [topic] explains the transformation of cause and effect. Jing says:
Regarding the statement that afflictions, karma, and birth all have afflictions as their cause:
from the seeds of affliction, present afflictions arise;
this is the cause of arising.
From a presently arisen affliction arises a presently arisen affliction;
this is the productive cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
From a presently arisen affliction arises a presently arisen action, provided it functions as a cause.
It is also an inducing cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
That which arises from the seeds of unwholesome afflictions as a retribution is an attracting cause (*ākarṣaṇa-hetu*).
There is also that which arises from the seeds of karma as a manifest emergence;
this is the cause of arising.
From the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma, retribution is produced.
This is the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
Furthermore, the afflictions that serve as the causal nature for the arising of manifest unwholesome karma are also the productive cause (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*).
Regarding the statement that "the fruit is likewise to be understood accordingly":
from the seeds of the five members of dependent origination,
there arises the future fruit of birth, aging, and death.
That which arises from maturation and produces further maturation is the productive cause (*janana-hetu*).
That which arises from maturation and gives rise to afflictions and karma is the appropriating cause (*parigraha-hetu*).
Because the dharmas produced by the three conditions are remote.
Master Ji says:
"A portion of the unwholesome afflictions of the desire realm have retributive results (*vipāka-phala*)," and so forth.
This refers to the unwholesome afflictions of ordinary beings that are abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
or, as for those unwholesome states within the continuum of one who has entered the noble state or a noble being,
they are subject to cessation through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and lack any ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
Furthermore, because the indeterminate afflictions of the desire realm do not transcend the fruit [of rebirth],
the fourth explanation concerns the transformation of deluded conduct.
This is as previously listed in seven types in the *Maulī Bhūmi*, as found in the eighth fascicle.
There is a name but no explanation.
Jingyun says:
"The three types of wrong views regarding the self."
Regarding the object, there are distinct modes of understanding that involve conceiving of a self, conceiving of annihilation, and repudiating existence;
these do not accord with correct reasoning.
This is termed "erroneous comprehension.
Ignorance (*avidyā*), as a single category, is by nature darkness and delusion;
it possesses no distinct mode of activity or understanding.
It is called "non-comprehension" (a-parijñā).
When doubt arises as to whether [an object] exists or not, it is called "comprehension" (parijñā);
when false understanding arises, it is called "non-comprehension."
The grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consists in regarding various views as supreme;
the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists in adhering to the prohibitions and precepts associated with those views and being attached to one's own view.
Because they harbor resentment toward the views of others,
they are all termed those who adhere to false comprehension;
for that which is false comprehension is precisely [the nature of] the various views.
The origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*) is precisely all of this.
If there are causes, conditions, lineages, and bases for arising,
then one becomes deluded regarding these and gives rise to all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, it is said that this is the conduct that serves as the basis for delusion regarding those causes and conditions;
cessation and the path are dharmas that oppose [delusion],
or one may feel fear toward them.
This [state] also arises from delusion;
therefore, it is said that these delusions give rise to the formations of fear regarding that.
Now, the doubt is resolved.
Regarding the doubt as to whether the Truths are understood or not understood: Kuiji states that when the three— view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*),
extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*)— give rise to erroneous conduct toward their objects...

These are exclusively afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and not of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) do not arise through delusion regarding the [four] truths.
This treatise states: "They function through delusion regarding the four noble truths."
They arise solely by taking the Four Noble Truths as their object;
other afflictions such as greed arise by taking these views as their object.
In the preceding four sections, the afflictions were presented individually.
It does not inquire into the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take untainted conditioned phenomena as their object.
In the fifth and sixth sections, the four truths and the six afflictions are explained individually;
herein, suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are the objects of the afflictions.
It is called the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) because it increases within the associated [mental states].
It is called "terror" because it eliminates afflictions through the cessation and the path.
The seventh category is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Since it arises spontaneously and does not arise from delusion regarding the truths (*satya*),
one knows that the preceding six categories are abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*).
The following section concludes the preceding discussion and introduces the subsequent section.
Jing says: "That is to say, as previously stated."
Regarding the distinctions between delusion concerning the Four Truths, delusion concerning what is to be abandoned through cultivation, and the relationship between obstacles and their remedies:
this merely follows what was appropriate for the transformation [of beings], being intended to facilitate the easy understanding of sentient beings;
thus, it concludes the preceding section.
Regarding the phrase "now, to explain them collectively," this refers to the sixth section below;
it shall be analyzed in detail within the eight questions and answers concerning the characteristics of severing afflictions (*kleśa*).
The explanation provided above has merely demonstrated the coarse characteristics.
Now, we shall analyze in detail the various categories, such as those with objects and those without objects;
this is not a direct exposition within the sixth category.
The third is the section explaining the objects (*vastu*).
This consists of three categories.
First, the five views and pride are termed "without object" (*avastuka*).
This means that because the self-entity which is the object of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not exist, it is called "without a real basis" (*avastuka*).
Because the other four views and pride arise in dependence upon the view of a self, they are also called "without a real basis.
The two types of greed and hatred, which arise in relation to the slightly pure and the impure, are called "with a real basis" (*sāvastuka*).
The three— ignorance, doubt,
and [wrong view]— when associated with [wrong] view and so forth, are termed "without objective basis" (avastuka);
when associated with craving and so forth, they are termed "with objective basis" (savastuka).
In principle, attachment and the other afflictions also pertain to non-existent objects;
therefore, the Abhidharma states:
"The view of self, pride, and craving are termed having non-existent objects."
Now, three categories are taught based on the majority of cases.
Jing says: "Among the seven types of pride, 'pride' (māna) and 'inferiority-pride' (ūnamāna) are excluded."
The remaining five types of pride have non-existent objects as their basis,
because they do not accord with reality;
the remaining two types of pride have existent objects as their basis.
However, speaking from the majority of cases, pride (*māna*) is said to be without an objective basis (*avastuka*).
Apang says: "For now, this is explained with reference to the pride of self (*asmimāna*), which is said to have no objective basis."
In terms of ultimate reality,

it also applies to that which has an objective basis (*savastuka*). As for the statement, "In reality there is no self, yet conceptualization proceeds," this sentence provides a general explanation of what was said above.
The views and pride are said to be "without a real object" (avastuka) in meaning.
In reality, even the conceit of self (asmimāna) takes a real object as its condition;
however, here they are specifically described such that pride is termed "without a real object" and craving is termed "with a real object."
Because they are mutually revealed through ellipsis and implication,
although the objects of the two types of grasping and so forth do indeed have substantial existence,
they arise with the view of self as their fundamental basis.
Furthermore, because it increases conceptual engagement (*vikalpa*), it is called "without an object" (*an-artha*).
However, the textual passages clarifying "with an object" (*sa-artha*) and "without an object" differ;
as the *Abhidharma* states:
The pride of views (*dṛṣṭi-māna*) is without an object, while the others possess objects.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states in one place that views, pride, and craving are without objects;
in another passage, it says that views and their associated factors are without objects.
The "views" [referred to here] are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
This treatise states at [verse] 58 that those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) have no objective basis (*avastuka*),
whereas the remaining [afflictions] share both having and not having an objective basis (*savastuka* and *avastuka*).
Fifty-nine states that views and pride have no objective basis (*avastuka*),
while greed and hatred have an objective basis (*sāvastuka*); doubt and ignorance pertain to both.
How are these various passages to be reconciled?
The Tripitaka Master says:
"They are to be reconciled according to the text of the *Nyāyānusāra*."
That treatise states: "As the Sūtra says:
'The afflictions abandoned through seeing have no objective basis as their object;
the afflictions abandoned through cultivation have an objective basis as their object.'"
There are three explanations for this scriptural passage.
The first states:
the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is called "without basis" and "without reality" because it refers to a self that does not exist.
The other afflictions abandoned through insight are also said to be "without objective basis" because they take the view of self and [the view of] mine as their root;
however, those abandoned through cultivation do not take the view of self as their root,
and are therefore said to be "with objective basis."
The second [teacher] says:
among the four views, one is the superimposition of what does not exist,
and the other is the denial of what exists.
However, because the correct principle (nyāya) involves no increase or decrease of entities,
the afflictions abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) are said to be "without entity" (avastuka);
whereas the afflictions abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) involve the grasping of increase or decrease, they are said to be "with entity" (savastuka).
Third, it is said:
Within the principle of the Four Noble Truths, there are no coarse or manifest phenomena;
therefore, the delusions that obscure them are called "without objective basis" (avastuka).
The afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation take coarse and manifest phenomena as their objects;
therefore, they are said to "have an object.
In the Mahāyāna school, for instance, it is stated in the *Pañcāśatikā* (Fifty Verses) that: [and so forth].
The afflictions abandoned through seeing are called "without a basis" (avastuka) because this is stated according to their fundamental nature.
As for those abandoned through cultivation, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, they lack the nature of views.
It is said that only that which is real exists;
since I also hold such a view, it is further said that there is no objective basis for my position.
Therefore, it is said that [the term] "penetration" applies to both.
The remaining passages should be interpreted according to this principle.
Fourth is the explanation of the gate of the association of faculties (*indriya-saṃprayoga*).
Jingyun: If those that arise spontaneously are all obtainable within the three feelings,

then those that arise spontaneously are obtained only on the mental level (*manobhūmi*) and are associated with the three faculties of sorrow (*daurmanasya*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding those that pervade all groups of consciousness and are associated with all faculties:
this refers to greed, hatred, and ignorance being associated with feeling (*vedanā*).
From "they do not arise spontaneously" up to "I shall now explain."
This is a general statement granting permission to explain the meaning of the association of the roots of afflictions arising from discrimination (*vikalpaja*).
Below follows the specific explanation of that association.
Regarding the phrase, "Greed is at one time associated with pleasure and joy," and so forth:
Tài says: This passage generally explains that the greed of the six consciousnesses is entirely associated with sorrow, joy, and so forth at one and the same time.
Question: How can anger that arises spontaneously be associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
Why is it that among those [afflictions] arising from discrimination (*vikalpaja*), association with equanimity (*upekṣā-samprayukta*) is not mentioned?
T’ai says: “In principle, it is actually mentioned, but it is omitted here for the sake of brevity.”

Regarding "pleasure associated only with the aggregate of formations" (*saṃskāra-skandha*): this refers to the pleasure associated with the aggregate of formations within the retributive states of humans and devas.

Regarding "suffering associated with the aggregate of formations": this refers to the suffering associated with the aggregate of formations in the three evil destinies. As for "abandonment being contrary to both [the views of] annihilationism and eternalism": [it is so because it transcends both].
Regarding the aggregates associated with pleasure, one conceives of the self as being annihilated, which is associated with sorrow;
regarding the aggregates associated with suffering, one conceives of the self as being annihilated, which is associated with joy and pleasure.
Because the two types of grasping take those views as their object, they are associated accordingly with those [feelings].
The view-grasping (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) is associated with whichever faculties correspond to the views as they are grasped.
The precept-and-vow-grasping (śīlavrataparāmarśa) is likewise associated with whichever faculties correspond to the precepts and vows as they are grasped.
In reality, false view is also associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*),
but it is not mentioned here because the exposition is abbreviated.
Within the category of pride (*māna*), there are likewise three types of inferiority.
It is omitted and not explained because it is easily understood.
Regarding matters such as gain and offerings that are certain to exist, when others speak to one saying, "This does not exist," doubt arises;
from this hesitation, anxiety is born.
One rejoices because there is no hesitation regarding gain and so forth, up to the speech of others concerning the miserable destinies.

Question: Thus far, greed and the other [afflictions] have been associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and physical pain (*duḥkha*); are they now characterized by joy (*prīti*) or by dejection (*daurmanasya*)?
The original text has not been seen.
There are three interpretations of its meaning. One says:
The faculties are categorized according to their underlying afflictions; since sorrow and suffering follow from craving,
they are subsumed under the nature of delight.
The second [master] says:
Since the delusions arise from the root of greed and depend upon sorrow and suffering, they are subsumed under the nature of distress.
The third says:
According to its essential nature,
it has multiple functions within a single moment; therefore,
sorrow and suffering arise conditioned by disagreeable objects.
They are subsumed under the nature of aversion (*daurmanasya*).
Because greed takes favorable objects as its condition, it is called the nature of elation (*prīti*).
